Biotic homogenisation between two surveys

Source: R/invasion.R
div_homogenisation.Rd

div_homogenisation() asks whether communities have become more alike over time, as when widespread alien species spread and local endemics are lost (biotic homogenisation; McKinney and Lockwood 1999; Olden and Rooney 2006). It computes the mean pairwise similarity among the same sites in two surveys (Jaccard or Sorensen, presence-absence) and the change, \(\Delta = \bar S_{after} - \bar S_{before}\): positive values mean homogenisation, negative values differentiation.

Site pairs share sites, so they are not independent. The confidence interval therefore resamples sites (a site bootstrap): sites are drawn with replacement, and the change is recomputed over the pairs of distinct drawn sites.

With status, the change is also computed with native species only: the difference between the two (alien_contribution) is the part of the change due to alien species.

Usage

div_homogenisation(
  before,
  after,
  site = site,
  species = species,
  status = NULL,
  alien = c("alien", "introduced", "exotic", "non-native", "invasive"),
  index = c("jaccard", "sorensen"),
  nboot = 999,
  conf = 0.95,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

before, after

Long-format data of the two surveys.

site, species

<tidy-select> The column holding site identifiers and the column holding species names.

status

Column giving each record's status. Values in alien count as alien; all others as native.

alien

Values of status that mean alien (default "alien", "introduced", "exotic", "non-native", "invasive").

index

"jaccard" or "sorensen" similarity.

nboot

Number of bootstrap resamples of sites.

conf

Confidence level.

seed

Optional random seed.

Value

A tibble with one row per species set ("all" and, with status, "native"): species_set, sites, similarity_before, similarity_after, change, lower, upper (bootstrap interval of the change); with status, an attribute alien_contribution.

References

McKinney, M. L. and Lockwood, J. L. (1999). Biotic homogenization: a few winners replacing many losers in the next mass extinction. Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 14, 450-453.

Olden, J. D. and Rooney, T. P. (2006). On defining and quantifying biotic homogenization. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 15, 113-120.

Examples

# A small illustrative example: one alien species spreads to every site
before <- data.frame(
  site = rep(1:4, each = 2),
  species = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h"),
  status = "native"
)
after <- rbind(before, data.frame(site = 1:4, species = "x", status = "alien"))
div_homogenisation(before, after, status = status, nboot = 99, seed = 1)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   species_set sites similarity_before similarity_after change lower upper
#>   <chr>       <int>             <dbl>            <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 all             4                 0              0.2    0.2   0.2   0.2
#> 2 native          4                 0              0      0     0     0
